passage:
The following text is from Sara Teasdale's poem "There Will Come Soft Rains," first published in 1918.

There will come soft rains and the smell of the ground, / And swallows circling with their shimmering sound; / And frogs in the pools singing at night, / And wild plum-trees in tremulous white; / Robins will wear their feathery fire / Whistling their whims on a low fence-wire; / And not one will know of the war, not one / Will care at last when it is done. / Not one would mind, neither bird nor tree / If mankind perished utterly; / And Spring herself, when she woke at dawn, / Would scarcely know that we were gone.
question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.text: The speaker describes the destruction caused by a war and then pleads with the natural world to restore what has been lost.
The speaker lists signs of each of the four seasons in turn and then asks which of them will outlast the others.
The speaker imagines a distant future in which people have at last learned to live in harmony with the natural world that they once thoughtlessly ignored.
The speaker accumulates images of a springtime landscape and then reveals that the scene continues, indifferent, after humanity has disappeared.

explanation:
**Choice D is correct.** The poem's first six lines pile up spring images, rains, swallows, frogs, plum blossom, robins, and its last six lines deliver the turn: none of these would notice the war, or notice "if mankind perished utterly."

**The Full Solution:**
- Structure half one: an accumulating catalog, each item introduced with "And," of a spring that "will come."
- Structure half two: the repeated "not one" pivots the catalog into a claim of indifference, culminating in Spring herself scarcely knowing "that we were gone."
- D tracks both movements: accumulation, then the reveal of a world going on without us.

**Why the other choices are wrong:**
- A: No destruction is described and nothing is asked of nature; the war exists only as the thing nature will not notice.
- B: Every image belongs to spring; no cycle of four seasons appears, and no question is posed.
- C: The poem's future contains no reconciled humanity; its point is that humanity may be absent altogether.

_meta.source: Sara Teasdale, "There Will Come Soft Rains" (1918), collected in Flame and Shadow (1920)
